claim: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder leading to progressive cognitive decline.
source: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder leading to progressive cognitive decline.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about AD being the most common neurodegenerative disorder.

claim: Heme-binding protein 1 (Hebp1) is elevated in the brains of both 3×Tg-AD mice and patients affected by rapidly-progressing forms of AD.
source: We show that one of these markers, heme-binding protein 1 (Hebp1), is elevated in the brains of both 3×Tg-AD mice and patients affected by rapidly-progressing forms of AD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry, immunoblotting, and immunohistochemistry presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hebp1 is predominantly expressed in neurons.
source: Hebp1, predominantly expressed in neurons, interacts with the mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS) and exhibits a perimitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical co-staining data showing Hebp1 expression in Ctip2-positive neurons but not in GFAP-positive astrocytes or Iba-1-positive microglia.

claim: Hebp1 interacts with the mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS).
source: Hebp1, predominantly expressed in neurons, interacts with the mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS) and exhibits a perimitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry and immunoblotting showing interaction with Mic60.

claim: Hebp1 exhibits a perimitochondrial localization.
source: Hebp1, predominantly expressed in neurons, interacts with the mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS) and exhibits a perimitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation, mitochondria isolation, and live imaging data showing Hebp1 association with mitochondria.

claim: Wildtype neurons show elevated cytotoxicity in response to heme-induced apoptosis.
source: Strikingly, wildtype, but not Hebp1-deficient, neurons showed elevated cytotoxicity in response to heme-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assays using MultiTox-Glo reagent showing increased cell death in wildtype neurons treated with hemin.

claim: Hebp1-deficient neurons do not show elevated cytotoxicity in response to heme-induced apoptosis.
source: Strikingly, wildtype, but not Hebp1-deficient, neurons showed elevated cytotoxicity in response to heme-induced apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assays showing no significant cell death in Hebp1-deficient neurons treated with hemin.

claim: Increased survivability in Hebp1-deficient neurons is conferred by blocking the activation of the mitochondrial-associated caspase signaling pathway.
source: Increased survivability in Hebp1-deficient neurons is conferred by blocking the activation of the mitochondrial-associated caspase signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that procaspase 9 was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons upon hemin treatment, and caspase 3/7 activity remained low.

claim: Hebp1 plays a role in progressive neuronal loss during AD progression.
source: Taken together, our data highlight a role of Hebp1 in progressive neuronal loss during AD progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing Hebp1 upregulation in AD and its role in mediating heme-induced neuronal apoptosis.

claim: AD is projected to affect more than 40 million people worldwide.
source: It is the most prevalent form of dementia in the elderly and is projected to affect more than 40 million people worldwide (GBD , Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study on disease prevalence.

claim: AD is characterized by disturbed metabolism of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides that results in formation of toxic oligomers and insoluble aggregates (plaques).
source: At the molecular level, AD is characterized by a disturbed metabolism of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides that results in formation of toxic oligomers and insoluble aggregates (plaques) in the brains of afflicted individuals (Selkoe and Hardy, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature on AD pathology.

claim: AD pathology is accompanied by formation of neurofibrillary tangles comprising of hyperphosphorylated microtubule-associated protein tau.
source: AD pathology is also accompanied by formation of neurofibrillary tangles comprising of hyperphosphorylated microtubule-associated protein tau.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: Aβ deposits and phospho-tau-containing neurofibrils serve as molecular hallmarks of AD and are useful for histopathological diagnosis.
source: Aβ deposits and phospho-tau-containing neurofibrils serve as molecular hallmarks of AD and are thus useful for histopathological diagnosis (Vinters, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on AD diagnosis.

claim: The aggregation of Aβ and tau alone does not fully account for the cognitive decline observed in AD patients.
source: However, the aggregation of Aβ and tau alone does not fully account for the cognitive decline observed in AD patients (Davis et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP) and its proteases presenilin-1 and 2 have a causative relationship with the onset of familiar form of Alzheimer's disease (FAD).
source: Although mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP) and its proteases presenilin-1 and 2 have a causative relationship with the onset of familiar form of Alzheimer's disease (FAD), overt manifestation of clinical AD is often preceded by a prolonged incubation period (Ryman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on familial AD.

claim: Overt manifestation of clinical AD is often preceded by a prolonged incubation period.
source: Although mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP) and its proteases presenilin-1 and 2 have a causative relationship with the onset of familiar form of Alzheimer's disease (FAD), overt manifestation of clinical AD is often preceded by a prolonged incubation period (Ryman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: 3×Tg-AD transgenic mice harbor three mutated genes associated with the disease (PSEN1 M146V, APP Swe, MAPT (tau) P301L).
source: To identify such markers, we probed for temporal changes in the brain proteome of 3×Tg-AD transgenic mice that harbor three mutated genes associated with the disease (PSEN1 M146V, APP Swe, MAPT (tau) P301L).
evidence: This is a description of the mouse model used in the study.

claim: 3×Tg-AD mice develop Alzheimer-related phenotypes in a progressive manner mimicking the human disorder.
source: These mice develop Alzheimer-related phenotypes in a progressive manner mimicking the human disorder (Oddo et al., 2003a; Oddo et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on the 3×Tg-AD mouse model.

claim: A total of 3760 protein groups were identified in the soluble brain protein fraction.
source: Analysis of the datasets using MaxQuant software (Cox and Mann, 2008), applying a peptide and protein false discovery rate (FDR) of 1%, identified a total of 3760 protein groups in the soluble brain protein fraction (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Between 2414 and 2574 proteins were quantified depending on the time point.
source: Of these, only proteins that were identified in at least two out of four biological replicates for each group (disease or control) at each time point were used for further analyses. In this way, between 2414 and 2574 proteins were quantified depending on the time point.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: Pearson's correlation coefficients for quantified proteins between biological replicates were above 0.96.
source: Pearson's correlation coefficients for quantified proteins between biological replicates were above 0.96 attesting to the high reproducibility of the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed that proteins can be clustered according to age (component 1, 40.9% of total variation) as well as disease state (component 2, 18.3% of total variation).
source: Principal component analysis of the datasets revealed that these proteins can be clustered according to age (component 1, 40.9% of total variation) as well as disease state (component 2, 18.3% of total variation) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increasing difference between control and AD brain proteome could be observed with aging and disease progression.
source: Notably, increasing difference between control and AD brain proteome could be observed with aging and disease progression (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The segregation by age was mainly driven by extracellular matrix proteins (Hapln2, Tnc, Acan, Vcan, Hapln1) and increased expression of microglia markers (S100b, Ctpd).
source: The segregation by age was mainly driven by extracellular matrix proteins (Hapln2, Tnc, Acan, Vcan, Hapln1) and increased expression of microglia markers (S100b, Ctpd) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by PCA loading analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Many of the proteins driving age segregation have been previously reported as markers of brain aging.
source: Many of these proteins have been previously reported as markers of brain aging (Sato and Endo, 2010; Végh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on brain aging markers.

claim: APP and tau (MAPT) were clustered together with proteins upregulated in AD.
source: As expected, APP and tau (MAPT) were clustered together with proteins upregulated in AD (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by PCA loading analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cumulative upregulation in expression of proteins involved in cell death and apoptotic processes could be detected at the first symptomatic time point (6 months).
source: Remarkably, cumulative upregulation in expression of proteins involved in cell death and apoptotic processes could already be detected at the first symptomatic time point (6 months) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Signatures of mitochondria dysfunction were among the very first signs of altered AD proteome.
source: Signatures of mitochondria dysfunction were also among the very first signs of altered AD proteome (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Significant changes in regulation of proteins associated with seizures were observed at the transition point between presymptomatic phase and 6 months.
source: Significant changes in regulation of proteins associated with seizures were also observed at the transition point between presymptomatic phase and 6 months which corresponds to the stage where changes in long-term potentiation (LTP) in 3×Tg-AD mice were previously described (Oddo et al., 2003b; Palop et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and citations to published research on LTP changes in 3×Tg-AD mice.

claim: Neurodegeneration-related processes (amyloid load of hippocampus, demyelination of axons and degradation of mitochondria) were noticeably exacerbated with AD progression.
source: Neurodegeneration-related processes (amyloid load of hippocampus, demyelination of axons and degradation of mitochondria) were also noticeably exacerbated with AD progression (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Disturbance of the cytoskeleton became prominent only at the late stage of the disorder (18 months).
source: Notably, disturbance of the cytoskeleton, which is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative disorders including AD, became prominent only at the late stage of the disorder (18 months) (Figure 2C) and correlated with the emergence of hyperphosphorylated tau in 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis in Figure 2C and tau phosphorylation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disturbance of the cytoskeleton correlated with the emergence of hyperphosphorylated tau in 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: Notably, disturbance of the cytoskeleton, which is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative disorders including AD, became prominent only at the late stage of the disorder (18 months) (Figure 2C) and correlated with the emergence of hyperphosphorylated tau in 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and tau phosphorylation data.

claim: Mutant tau, APP and PSEN1 were principally responsible for the differences observed between wild-type and 3×Tg-AD brains.
source: To identify the primary drivers of the phenotypes observed at each stage, identification of top upstream regulators was performed using IPA. This revealed that mutant tau, APP and PSEN1 were principally responsible for the differences observed between wild-type and 3×Tg-AD brains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by upstream regulator analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The proteins that are regulated by tau, APP and PSEN1 largely overlap.
source: Interestingly, the proteins that are regulated by tau, APP and PSEN1 in our dataset largely overlap (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Downstream effectors of tau, APP and PSEN1 contribute primarily to apoptosis, mitochondria dysfunction and oxidative stress.
source: Protein enrichment by biological function indicates that these downstream effectors contribute primarily to apoptosis, mitochondria dysfunction and oxidative stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Several proteins involved in mRNA processing (Hnrnpm, Hnrnpl, Nono, Matrin3) were strongly upregulated at the later time points.
source: For instance, several proteins involved in mRNA processing (Hnrnpm, Hnrnpl, Nono, Matrin3) were strongly upregulated at the later time points.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing increased expression of these proteins.

claim: Expression of mRNA processing proteins increased gradually in coordinated manner throughout the progression of the disorder.
source: Remarkably, expression of these proteins increased gradually in coordinated manner throughout the progression of the disorder (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by time-course expression data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A group of serine protease inhibitors (Serpina1c, Serpina3k, Mug1) were significantly downregulated by the latest time point examined.
source: A similar coordinated expression pattern was also observed for the group of serine protease inhibitors (Serpina1c, Serpina3k, Mug1) which were significantly downregulated by the latest time point examined (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by time-course expression data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: A reduction in protease inhibitors levels has been linked to aging and cognitive decline.
source: This result is particularly interesting in light of recent findings linking a reduction in protease inhibitors levels to aging and cognitive decline (Castellano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Several inflammation-related proteins (C1qc, Ilf2, Igh-3) and components of myelin sheath (Mag, Mog) were strongly up- or downregulated at the preterminal stage of the disorder (18 months).
source: We have also identified several inflammation-related proteins (C1qc, Ilf2, Igh-3) and components of myelin sheath (Mag, Mog) to be strongly up- or downregulated at the preterminal stage of the disorder (18 months).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data at the 18-month time point.

claim: Progressive inflammation and demyelination have been linked to AD.
source: This hints towards progressive inflammation and demyelination in the analyzed 3×Tg-AD model which has been linked to AD (Wyss-Coray and Rogers, 2012; Zhan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on inflammation and demyelination in AD.

claim: Half of the identified putative early markers were previously associated with AD or other neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Noteworthy, half of the identified putative early markers were previously associated with AD or other neurodegenerative disorders (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by literature review summarized in Table 1.

claim: Decreased levels of ApoA1 have been linked to the increased severity of AD in human patients.
source: For example, decreased levels of ApoA1 that we observe in our dataset have been linked to the increased severity of AD in human patients (Merched et al., 2000; Saczynski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ApoA1 in AD.

claim: Guanosine monophosphate reductase 1 (Gmpr) was identified to be expressed at increased levels in the brains of AD patients.
source: Guanosine monophosphate reductase 1 (Gmpr) which was identified to be expressed at increased levels in the brains of AD patients followed the same direction of change in our dataset (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Gmpr in AD.

claim: Glyoxalase-1 (Glo1) was previously shown to be upregulated in other mouse models of neurodegeneration.
source: Glyoxalase-1 (Glo1), another protein whose elevated expression was detected in our study, was previously shown to be upregulated in other mouse models of neurodegeneration (Chen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Glo1 in neurodegeneration.

claim: Restoration of Glo1 activity has been proposed as a mechanism to combat cognitive dysfunction in AD.
source: Furthermore, restoration of Glo1 activity has been proposed as a mechanism to combat cognitive dysfunction in AD (More et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Glo1 as a therapeutic target.

claim: Hebp1 was the most highly and consistently upregulated protein at all time points.
source: Among the newly identified putative presymptomatic markers of AD, heme-binding protein 1 (Hebp1) is a particularly interesting candidate. In our dataset, it was the most highly and consistently upregulated protein at all time points.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing Hebp1 upregulation across all time points.

claim: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family.
source: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family and was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding protoporphyrin IX and heme (Jacob Blackmon et al., 2002; Dias et al., 2006; Taketani et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 protein family and function.

claim: Hebp1 was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding protoporphyrin IX and heme.
source: Hebp1 belongs to the SOUL protein family and was originally identified as a tetrapyrol-binding protein capable of binding protoporphyrin IX and heme (Jacob Blackmon et al., 2002; Dias et al., 2006; Taketani et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 function.

claim: Heme is essential for proper mitochondria function and cell survival.
source: Heme is essential for proper mitochondria function and cell survival (Atamna, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on heme function.

claim: Impairments in heme metabolism are associated with AD.
source: Impairments in heme metabolism are also associated with AD (Atamna and Frey, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on heme metabolism in AD.

claim: Cell survival and mitochondria function might be among the first pathways affected in AD.
source: Our data show that cell survival and mitochondria function might be among the first pathways affected in AD (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from pathway analysis data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An overall increase in expression of both Hebp1 and Glo1 was confirmed in AD patients compared to controls.
source: We could confirm an overall increase in expression of both proteins in AD patients compared to controls that validated our findings obtained in the 3×Tg-AD model.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of human postmortem brain samples.

claim: A strong difference in expression of Hebp1 and Glo1 was primarily observed in rapidly-progressing AD cases (death within 4 year period after diagnosis).
source: Interestingly, a strong difference in expression of Hebp1 and Glo1 was primarily observed in rapidly-progressing AD cases (death within 4 year period after diagnosis) (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis and quantification shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Rapidly-progressing AD cases are characterized by distinct pathological features and clinical parameters and are associated with a faster progression and more severe form of the disease.
source: These cases of AD are characterized by distinct pathological features and clinical parameters and are associated with a faster progression and more severe form of the disease (Chitravas et al., 2011; Zafar et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on rapidly-progressing AD.

claim: HEBP1 mRNA expression in prefrontal and primary visual cortex is significantly elevated in AD patients.
source: The datasets from Harvard Brain Tissue Resource Center (GN326, GN327, GN328) demonstrated significantly increased levels of HEBP1 mRNA in prefrontal and primary visual cortex in AD patients stressing a strong relevance of Hebp1 to AD in humans.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available mRNA expression datasets.

claim: Hebp1 was most abundant in the hippocampus, followed by the brain stem and cortical areas.
source: Immunoblot analyses of four brain areas in 12-month-old mice indicated that Hebp1 was most abundant in the hippocampus, followed by the brain stem and cortical areas (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Hebp1 was not detectable in the cerebellum.
source: Hebp1 was not detectable in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of brain regions.

claim: Hebp1 became dramatically elevated in all four brain regions in age matched 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: Significantly, Hebp1 became dramatically elevated in all four brain regions in age matched 3×Tg-AD mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed upregulated expression of Hebp1 in neocortex and hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice compared with wild-type controls.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed upregulated expression of Hebp1 in neocortex and hippocampus of 3×Tg-AD mice compared with wild-type controls (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hebp1 is strongly expressed in Ctip2-immunoreactive neurons.
source: Hebp1 is strongly expressed in Ctip2-immunoreactive neurons but is poorly associated with GFAP-stained astrocytes or Iba-1-labeled microglia in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hebp1 is poorly associated with GFAP-stained astrocytes or Iba-1-labeled microglia in the hippocampus.
source: Hebp1 is strongly expressed in Ctip2-immunoreactive neurons but is poorly associated with GFAP-stained astrocytes or Iba-1-labeled microglia in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hebp1 has been proposed to participate in transport of heme from mitochondria to cytosol.
source: Hebp1 has been proposed to participate in transport of heme from mitochondria to cytosol (Jacob Blackmon et al., 2002; Taketani et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 function.

claim: Heme-binding protein 2/SOUL, a homologue of Hebp1, is involved in mediation of cell death by recruitment to mitochondria permeability transition pore.
source: Furthermore, heme-binding protein 2/SOUL, a homologue of Hebp1, is involved in mediation of cell death by recruitment to mitochondria permeability transition pore (Szigeti et al., 2006; Szigeti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp2/SOUL function.

claim: Subcellular fractionation of the mouse brain indicated that Hebp1 is present in both synaptosomal (P2) and crude mitochondrial (Mt) fractions.
source: Subcellular fractionation of the mouse brain indicated that Hebp1 is present in both synaptosomal (P2) and crude mitochondrial (Mt) fractions where mitochondria are expected to be present (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hebp1 can be mitochondrially-associated as detected from mitochondria isolated from cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: We further demonstrated that the protein can be mitochondrially-associated by detecting the presence of Hebp1 from mitochondria isolated from cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondria isolation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A portion of EGFP-tagged Hebp1 expressed in rat primary neurons appears to be closely juxtaposed to mitochondria.
source: Supporting the biochemical data, we observed that a portion of EGFP-tagged Hebp1 expressed in rat primary neurons appears to be closely juxtaposed to mitochondria (visualized using Mitotracker) (Figure 5C and line scans in Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5C, 5E, and 5F.

claim: The signal from EGFP alone exhibited no correlated association with Mitotracker.
source: In comparison to this, the signal from EGFP alone exhibited no correlated association with Mitotracker (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The core components of mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), Mic60, Mic19 and Mic25, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
source: Interestingly, the core components of mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), Mic60, Mic19 and Mic25, as well as proteins of outer mitochondria membrane associated with MICOS complex, SAMM50 and Mtx2, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of co-immunoprecipitated proteins.

claim: Proteins of outer mitochondria membrane associated with MICOS complex, SAMM50 and Mtx2, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
source: Interestingly, the core components of mitochondrial contact site complex (MICOS), Mic60, Mic19 and Mic25, as well as proteins of outer mitochondria membrane associated with MICOS complex, SAMM50 and Mtx2, were enriched in Hebp1 Co-IP samples.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of co-immunoprecipitated proteins.

claim: The interaction between Hebp1 with Mic60 was confirmed by immunoblotting.
source: We further confirmed the interaction between Hebp1 with Mic60 by probing the immunoprecipitated complexes with their respective antibodies via immunoblotting (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot validation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hebp1 locates in close proximity to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it interacts with MICOS complex potentially through association with outer mitochondria membrane proteins such as SAMM50 or Mtx2.
source: Taken together these data indicate that Hebp1 locates in close proximity to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it interacts with MICOS complex potentially through association with outer mitochondria membrane proteins such as SAMM50 or Mtx2.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing enrichment of MICOS components and outer membrane proteins.

claim: A very similar pattern of subcellular localization was observed in cells that were transfected with full-length Hebp2/SOUL.
source: In line with our observations, a very similar pattern of subcellular localization was observed in cells that were transfected with full-length Hebp2/SOUL (Szigeti et al., 2006), further hinting towards potential role of Hebp1 in the regulation of cell death.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Hebp2/SOUL localization.

claim: Dysregulation of proteins linked to heme metabolism has been reported in AD.
source: Dysregulation of proteins linked to heme metabolism has been reported in AD (Hani Atamna & Frey, 2004; Schipper et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on heme metabolism in AD.

claim: Aβ can form a complex with heme which possesses strong peroxidase and superoxide activities that can contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity during AD.
source: Moreover, Aβ can form a complex with heme which possesses strong peroxidase and superoxide activities that can contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity during AD (Atamna and Boyle, 2006; Chiziane et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Aβ-heme complexes.

claim: Accumulation of Aβ around brain vasculature results in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), microvessel destruction and leakage of free heme into brain tissue.
source: Accumulation of Aβ around brain vasculature results in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), microvessel destruction and leakage of free heme into brain tissue (Chiziane et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on CAA and heme leakage.

claim: High concentrations of free heme are toxic to multiple cell types.
source: Due to its strong hydrophobicity, heme is almost exclusively bound to carrier proteins within cells. High concentrations of free heme are toxic to multiple cell types (Gemelli et al., 2014; Owen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on heme toxicity.

claim: Hebp1 was successfully eliminated in rat hippocampal neurons using CRISPR/Cas9 using three different gRNA sequences.
source: To test this hypothesis, we successfully eliminated expression of Hebp1 in rat hippocampal neurons using CRISPR/Cas9 using three different gRNA sequences (Figure 7A, KO1-3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing loss of Hebp1 expression in Figure 7A.

claim: Treatment of wildtype and control neurons with hemin resulted in 2.69 (±0.15) and 2.86 (±0.23) fold increase in cell death respectively as compared to exposure to vehicle only.
source: Consistent with the cytotoxic effects of high heme levels, treatment of wildtype (WT) and control neurons (LUC) with hemin resulted in 2.69 (±0.15) and 2.86 (±0.23) fold increase in cell death for WT and LUC respectively as compared to exposure to vehicle only (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Hebp1-deficient neurons exhibited no significant cell death in response to hemin treatment.
source: Strikingly, Hebp1-deficient neurons exhibited no significant cell death.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data showing no increase in cell death in Hebp1-KO neurons.

claim: The protective effect of Hebp1 deficiency against hemin-induced cell death was consistently observed in both gRNA sequences used.
source: This effect was consistently observed in both the gRNA sequences used (Figure 7B, KO1 and KO2).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: All 3 groups of neurons exhibited increased levels of cellular toxicity in response to tert-butyl-hydroperoxide or staurosporine.
source: As expected, all 3 groups of neurons exhibited increased levels of cellular toxicity, confirming that loss of Hebp1 is protective towards hemin-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Loss of Hebp1 is protective towards hemin-induced cytotoxicity.
source: As expected, all 3 groups of neurons exhibited increased levels of cellular toxicity, confirming that loss of Hebp1 is protective towards hemin-induced cytotoxicity (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of the protective effect to hemin but not other apoptosis inducers.

claim: Endogenous levels of Hebp1 are sufficient to trigger neuronal cell death that is influenced by heme concentrations.
source: These results indicate that endogenous levels of Hebp1 are sufficient to trigger neuronal cell death that is, in turn, influenced by heme concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that overexpression did not significantly increase cytotoxicity beyond endogenous levels.

claim: Reduction of Mic60 in cells has been associated with release of Cytochrome C (CytC) and increased sensitivity to apoptosis triggers.
source: In particular, reduction of Mic60 in cells has been associated with release of Cytochrome C (CytC) and increased sensitivity to apoptosis triggers (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Mic60 function.

claim: Release of CytC is often associated with loss of mitochondrial potential and is followed by Apaf1 activation and the ensuing conversion of procaspase 9 into caspase 9 and procaspase 3 into caspase 3.
source: Release of CytC, often associated with loss of mitochondrial potential, is followed by Apaf1 activation and the ensuing conversion of procaspase 9 into caspase 9 and procaspase 3 into caspase 3, thereby committing the cells into apoptosis (Franklin and Robertson, 2007; Zou et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on apoptosis mechanisms.

claim: Exposure of neurons to hemin decreases mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in wildtype, control as well as Hebp1-deficient neurons.
source: Indeed, exposure of neurons to hemin decreases mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) in wildtype, control as well as Hebp1-deficient neurons (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial membrane potential assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A steeper decrease in MMP was observed in Hebp1-deficient neurons (58.7 ± 2.83% and 60.9 ± 1.77% in KO1 and KO2 neurons) as compared to wildtype and control neurons (15.1 ± 2.77% and 14.1 ± 0.22%).
source: However, a steeper decrease in MMP was observed in Hebp1-deficient neurons (58.7 ± 2.83% and 60.9 ± 1.77% in KO1 and KO2 neurons) as compared to the other two groups (15.1 ± 2.77% and 14.1 ± 0.22% in wildtype and control neurons, respectively) strongly suggesting that effects on mitochondrial membrane potential alone cannot be the sole explanation for Hebp1's role in causing neuronal apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial membrane potential assay data.

claim: Effects on mitochondrial membrane potential alone cannot be the sole explanation for Hebp1's role in causing neuronal apoptosis.
source: However, a steeper decrease in MMP was observed in Hebp1-deficient neurons (58.7 ± 2.83% and 60.9 ± 1.77% in KO1 and KO2 neurons) as compared to the other two groups (15.1 ± 2.77% and 14.1 ± 0.22% in wildtype and control neurons, respectively) strongly suggesting that effects on mitochondrial membrane potential alone cannot be the sole explanation for Hebp1's role in causing neuronal apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hebp1-deficient neurons had greater MMP loss but were protected from apoptosis.

claim: CytC was released from mitochondria in all neurons (wildtype, control and Hebp1-deficient) treated with hemin.
source: Indeed, using mitochondria isolated from these neurons, we observe that CytC was released from these organelles in all neurons (wildtype, control and Hebp1-deficient) treated with hemin (Figure 8A and B), confirming that this step of mitochondria-associated apoptosis is not affected by loss of Hebp1 function.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: CytC release is not affected by loss of Hebp1 function.
source: Indeed, using mitochondria isolated from these neurons, we observe that CytC was released from these organelles in all neurons (wildtype, control and Hebp1-deficient) treated with hemin (Figure 8A and B), confirming that this step of mitochondria-associated apoptosis is not affected by loss of Hebp1 function.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis showing CytC release in all neuron types.

claim: Procaspase 9 was cleaved in wildtype and control neurons upon hemin-treatment.
source: Strikingly, we observe that while procaspase 9 was cleaved in wildtype and control neurons upon hemin-treatment, the protein was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Procaspase 9 was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons upon hemin-treatment.
source: Strikingly, we observe that while procaspase 9 was cleaved in wildtype and control neurons upon hemin-treatment, the protein was not activated in Hebp1-deficient neurons (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Hemin exposure caused a dramatic increase in the population of caspase 3+/7+ cells in wildtype (58.5 ± 2.89%) and control neurons (62.4 ± 1.88%) but not in Hebp1-deficient neurons (8.69 ± 1.55% and 9.86 ± 2.09% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
source: In agreement with this, hemin exposure caused a dramatic increase in the population of caspase 3+/7+ cells in wildtype (58.5 ± 2.89%) and control neurons (62.4 ± 1.88%) but not in Hebp1-deficient neurons (8.69 ± 1.55% and 9.86 ± 2.09% in KO1 and KO2, respectively) (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is supported by caspase 3/7 activity assay data shown in Figures 8D and 8E.

claim: Hebp1, found almost exclusively in the mitochondrial fraction in untreated wildtype and control neurons, was released from the mitochondria of these neurons upon exposure to hemin.
source: Noteworthy, Hebp1, found almost exclusively in the mitochondrial fraction in untreated wildtype and control neurons, was released from the mitochondria of these neurons upon exposure to hemin (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Release of mitochondrial Hebp1 in the presence of excessive heme is a critical trigger linking mitochondrial damage to neuronal apoptosis via activation of the procaspase 9 pathway.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that release of mitochondrial Hebp1 in the presence of excessive heme is a critical trigger linking mitochondrial damage to neuronal apoptosis via activation of the procaspase 9 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing Hebp1 release, lack of caspase 9 activation in Hebp1-deficient neurons, and protection from apoptosis.

claim: Mic60 was released from mitochondria, but only in Hebp1-deficient cells.
source: Interestingly, Mic60 was also released from mitochondria, but only in Hebp1-deficient cells, while Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet for all groups of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of mitochondrial and cytosolic fractions.

claim: Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet for all groups of neurons.
source: Interestingly, Mic60 was also released from mitochondria, but only in Hebp1-deficient cells, while Cox4 remained in the mitochondrial pellet for all groups of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis showing Cox4 as a mitochondrial marker.

claim: Cytotoxicity was observed in both wildtype (40.2 ± 1.23%) and control neurons (42.8 ± 1.15%) treated with Aβ42.
source: As expected, cytotoxicity was observed in both wildtype (40.2 ± 1.23%) and control neurons (42.8 ± 1.15%) treated with Aβ42 (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Concurrent exposure of wildtype and control neurons to Aβ42 and hemin caused an additional 2-fold increase in cytotoxicity (87.9 ± 1.04% for wildtype and 89.1 ± 0.63% for control neurons).
source: Concurrent exposure of these neurons to Aβ42 and hemin caused an additional 2-fold increase in cytotoxicity (87.9 ± 1.04% for wildtype and 89.1 ± 0.63% for control neurons), an additive effect presumably caused by formation of an Aβ-heme complex that can contribute to oxidative stress and cytotoxicity during AD (Atamna and Boyle, 2006; Chiziane et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data and citations to published research on Aβ-heme complexes.

claim: Very low levels of cytotoxicity were detected when Hebp1-KO neurons were exposed to Aβ42 alone (7.51 ± 0.70% and 7.29 ± 0.96% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
source: In contrast to this, very low levels of cytotoxicity were detected when Hebp1-KO neurons were exposed to Aβ42 alone (7.51 ± 0.70% and 7.29 ± 0.96% in KO1 and KO2, respectively), similar to hemin treatment (9.65 ± 0.77% and 9.42 ± 0.87% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data.

claim: Cytotoxicity levels remained low in Hebp1-KO neurons even after concurrent treatment with Aβ42 and hemin (22.9 ± 0.84% and 23.9 ± 0.84% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
source: Even more significantly, cytotoxicity levels remained low even after concurrent treatment with Aβ42 and hemin (22.9 ± 0.84% and 23.9 ± 0.84% in KO1 and KO2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data.

claim: Hebp1 participates in converging pathways triggered by Aβ42 and heme that cause cytotoxicity via apoptotic cell death in neurons.
source: Thus, Hebp1 participates in converging pathways triggered by Aβ42 and heme that cause cytotoxicity via apoptotic cell death in neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hebp1-deficient neurons are protected from both Aβ42 and hemin-induced cytotoxicity.

claim: Proteins related to cell death, mitochondria function and seizures are among the first affected in AD.
source: Our study indicated that proteins related to cell death, mitochondria function and seizures are among the first affected in AD.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of proteomic data at early time points.

claim: Alterations of cytoskeleton-related proteins became apparent only at the late stage of the disorder which coincides with the timeline of tau aggregation.
source: Alterations of cytoskeleton-related proteins became apparent only at the late stage of the disorder which coincides with the timeline of tau aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and tau phosphorylation data.

claim: Matrin-3 and Nono form a complex involved in DNA damage response and recognition and retention of incorrectly processed mRNA in nucleus.
source: These included proteins that are involved in mRNA processing such as Matrin-3 and Nono that form a complex involved in DNA damage response and recognition and retention of incorrectly processed mRNA in nucleus (Salton et al., 2010; Zhang and Carmichael, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Matrin-3 and Nono function.

claim: Hnrnpm and Hnrnpl regulate alternative splicing.
source: Similar expression patterns were detected for Hnrnpm and Hnrnpl, which regulate alternative splicing (Fei et al., 2017; Passacantilli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hnrnpm and Hnrnpl function.

claim: U1 snRNP components were found to be enriched in insoluble brain proteome of AD patients.
source: Bai and colleagues have previously found U1 snRNP components to be enriched in insoluble brain proteome of AD patients and demonstrated impaired splicing of AD-related transcripts (Bai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on U1 snRNP in AD.

claim: A recent study of the hippocampal proteome in the 5 × FAD mouse model of AD identified downregulation of serpins.
source: Interestingly, a recent study of the hippocampal proteome in the 5 × FAD mouse model of AD also identified downregulation of serpins (Gurel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on serpins in AD mouse models.

claim: Injection of recombinant metalloprotease inhibitor TIMP2 intraperitoneally to reach the brain improved the cognitive function of aged mice.
source: This approach was recently tested with metalloprotease inhibitor TIMP2 which was injected intraperitoneally to reach the brain and improve the cognitive function of aged mice (Castellano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on TIMP2 as a therapeutic approach.

claim: Hebp1 and Glo1 were highly elevated already at the presymptomatic stage in 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: The present study uncovered two proteins, Hebp1 and Glo1, that were highly elevated already at the presymptomatic stage in 3×Tg-AD mice, suggesting that they could be of potential relevance as early AD markers.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data at the 2-month time point.

claim: Hebp1 and Glo1 were expressed at significantly higher levels particularly in rapidly progressing cases of AD.
source: Both proteins were also expressed at significantly higher levels - particularly in rapidly progressing cases of AD - indicating that they could be of use to identify this group of patients.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis of human postmortem brain samples.

claim: Mic60 is an important player in cell death.
source: Interestingly, Mic60, a component of the MICOS complex that binds Hebp1, is also an important player in cell death.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mic60 function.

claim: Loss of Mic60 increases the rate of apoptosis due to dissipation of cristae junctions and intensifies leakage of CytC from mitochondria to cytosol.
source: Loss of Mic60 increases the rate of apoptosis due to dissipation of cristae junctions and intensifies leakage of CytC from mitochondria to cytosol (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on Mic60 function.

claim: SOUL, a homolog of Hebp1, promotes cell death presumably through permeabilization of mitochondria membranes.
source: Moreover, SOUL, a homolog of Hebp1, promotes cell death presumably through permeabilization of mitochondria membranes (Szigeti et al., 2006; Szigeti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on SOUL function.

claim: Loss of neurons is a key event leading to cognitive decline in AD and is mainly attributed to intensified apoptosis.
source: Loss of neurons is a key event leading to cognitive decline in AD and is mainly attributed to intensified apoptosis (Cotman and Su, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on neuronal loss in AD.

claim: Overexpression of proteins counteracting apoptotic response has been shown to decrease pathology in 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: Overexpression of proteins counteracting apoptotic response has been previously shown to decrease pathology in 3×Tg-AD mice (Rohn et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on anti-apoptotic interventions in AD mice.

claim: Degradation of heme by heme oxygenase-1 was demonstrated to reduce cytotoxicity caused by Aβ1–42 peptide.
source: Degradation of heme by heme oxygenase-1 was demonstrated to reduce cytotoxicity caused by Aβ1–42 peptide (Hettiarachchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on heme oxygenase-1 and Aβ toxicity.

claim: Heme synthesis is impaired in AD and accumulation of immature heme species can be a potential source of heme overload.
source: Heme synthesis is impaired in AD and accumulation of immature heme species can be a potential source of heme overload (Hani Atamna & Frey, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on heme synthesis in AD.

claim: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy contributes significantly to AD both in human and the 3×Tg-AD model starting from the early stage of the disorder.
source: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy contributes significantly to AD both in human and the 3×Tg-AD model starting from the early stage of the disorder (Ghiso et al., 2010; Li and Praticò, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on CAA in AD.

claim: Pathophysiological changes in brain vasculature have been reported in 3×Tg-AD mice.
source: Moreover, pathophysiological changes in brain vasculature have also been reported in 3×Tg-AD mice (Grammas et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on vascular changes in 3×Tg-AD mice.

claim: CAA may lead to disruption of brain vasculature and release of heme outside the vessels.
source: Thus, CAA may lead to disruption of brain vasculature and release of heme outside the vessels (Chiziane et al., 2018; Natté et al., 2001) and is also associated with apoptosis (Fossati et al., 2010; Mattson, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on CAA and heme release.

claim: CAA is associated with apoptosis.
source: Thus, CAA may lead to disruption of brain vasculature and release of heme outside the vessels (Chiziane et al., 2018; Natté et al., 2001) and is also associated with apoptosis (Fossati et al., 2010; Mattson, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on CAA and apoptosis.

claim: N-terminal cleavage of Hebp1 by cathepsin D results in generation of 21 amino acid long peptide called F2L that is capable of binding FPRL1/FPR2 receptor on the surface of mouse neutrophils and promote their migration.
source: Two previous publications demonstrated that N-terminal cleavage of Hebp1 by cathepsin D results in generation of 21 amino acid long peptide called F2L that is capable of binding FPRL1/FPR2 receptor on the surface of mouse neutrophils and promote their migration (Devosse et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hebp1 cleavage and F2L function.

claim: In the mouse brain, FPR2 is expressed predominantly by activated microglia.
source: In the mouse brain, FPR2 is expressed predominantly by activated microglia (Cui et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on FPR2 expression.

claim: FPRL1-positive microglia was shown to be recruited to Aβ plaques in AD patients.
source: Moreover, FPRL1-positive microglia was shown to be recruited to Aβ plaques in AD patients (Le et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on FPRL1-positive microglia in AD.

claim: Expression of cathepsin D strongly correlates with aging in the dataset.
source: In our dataset, expression of the Hebp1 protease cathepsin D also strongly correlates with aging which indicates the possibility of the progressive F2L accumulation in 3×Tg-AD mice with age.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data showing cathepsin D expression changes with age.

claim: Increased expression of cathepsin D in hippocampus of AD patients was reported previously.
source: Increased expression of cathepsin D in hippocampus of AD patients was also reported previously (Hondius et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on cathepsin D in AD.

claim: Cleavage of Hebp1 by cathepsin D in neurons may generate the soluble F2L peptide to recruit activated microglia and modulate inflammatory response during AD.
source: Thus, it is possible that cleavage of Hebp1 by cathepsin D in neurons may additionally generate the soluble F2L peptide to recruit activated microglia and modulate inflammatory response during AD.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the known functions of Hebp1, cathepsin D, and F2L.
